extracted.intended_audience: fiction writers (authors/screenwriters) working with ensemble casts or deciding point-of-view structure
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for planning, writing, and revising ensemble stories: deciding whether a story needs multiple POVs/characters, how to introduce and manage a cast, and how to use splitting/reuniting the team effectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Start by asking 'what is the story I'm trying to tell'
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish the story itself (the internal life/arc being represented) from who the story is about; identify whether the narrative requires an ensemble or a single protagonist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the core story is larger than one person's internal life, it may require multiple POVs or an ensemble (examples: The Inheritance of Orquidea Divina was expanded from a single POV to multiple; Cece Rios sequel became dual-POV when the story was 'too big'). Determine this early so scope and structure follow the story's needs rather than arbitrary character count.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include only the necessary team members
rubrics_metrics.description: If the plot requires a team effort from the heroes, make sure the necessary team members make it onto the page.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify the functions the plot requires (e.g., heist specialists) and cast characters to fill those functions. Don't add characters just because they're 'cool'—they must serve the story. Example: heist stories require specialists; failing to include needed roles weakens the plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid character-introduction bloat
rubrics_metrics.description: Character introductions are fun but can lead to bloat if overdone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Control the impulse to keep adding new characters (illustrated by X-Men era and Song of Ice and Fire's growing cast). Cut characters who are 'dead weight' or redundant with others. Editors often ask: 'Do you need another person?' Use that litmus test to trim the cast.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure each character brings unique, non-redundant value
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters should not be doing the exact same narrative work; avoid redundancy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If two characters perform identical roles, one may be unnecessary. Characters in ensembles should have distinct abilities, perspectives, or functions (e.g., the different specialists in a heist). Example anti-pattern: keeping multiple characters who do the same thing 'just because they're cool.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-establish investment and the group's purpose before breaking them apart
rubrics_metrics.description: Before splitting an ensemble, readers/viewers must be invested in the characters and understand why they form a collective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish a 'big win' or reason for the group's existence so that when they are separated, stakes and losses (e.g., death, separation) feel meaningful. Examples: Lord of the Rings and Fellowship — investment in the fellowship makes splits impactful; failing to pre-establish leads to unsatisfying outcomes (How I Met Your Mother ending).

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't split the ensemble just to reunite them — make the split do new work
rubrics_metrics.description: Splitting and then reuniting the team is formulaic unless the separation produces new revelations or developments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid using breakup/reunion solely as a payoff; instead use splits to explore character development, show unexpected pairings, delegate distinct tasks, or reveal new stakes. Anti-patterns: second-season rehashes (Heroes S2) where the same story beats repeat without new insight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use splitting to pair characters in new, revealing ways
rubrics_metrics.description: When you break an ensemble up, pair or group characters in unexpected combinations to reveal different facets of them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: DuckTales and Community use rare pairings to show sides of characters not normally seen. This creates fresh story opportunities and character growth (e.g., Lena with Huey revealed an unexpected arc).

rubrics_metrics.name: Let internal doubts answer the 'are we stronger together?' question
rubrics_metrics.description: You can explore whether characters belong to the ensemble by showing one character's internal realization they don't fit (the 'tin dog' moment), without physically breaking the team apart.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A character's soul-searching about usefulness (Doctor Who 'I'm the tin dog') can provide emotional depth and answer the ensemble question in ways other than separation. Use internal conflict to test group cohesion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use splits as opportunities to tell new stories and reveal new character dimensions
rubrics_metrics.description: Breaking the ensemble should open narrative space to tell stories you couldn't otherwise tell and deepen characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When characters are separated to accomplish different tasks (e.g., delegation to different locations like Mordor), each fragment should contribute new information or development that enriches the whole. If separation yields nothing new, readers will feel cheated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be intentional when introducing a new member to an established ensemble
rubrics_metrics.description: Bringing in a foreign or new character must disrupt and integrate the group in a meaningful way rather than feeling tacked on.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pre-established group dynamics make new entrants noticeable; to work, the newcomer should alter dynamics or help explore new themes. Poor integration (example: How I Met Your Mother struggles with integrating the mother) makes the addition feel unsatisfying.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on the desire for connection as a driving force for ensembles
rubrics_metrics.description: A core reason audiences are drawn to ensembles is characters' desire for connection; this desire should be evident and motivate interactions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flash's line 'I need friends' illustrates how a character's yearning to connect can hold a team together. Emphasize relational wants and vulnerabilities to make ensemble bonds compelling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create and use a connection map for practical management
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical exercise: map every character's relationships to one another, include at least one challenge in each relationship, and one way the relationship enhances each character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This 'connection' map helps track interactions, prevent redundancy, and identify sources of conflict and growth. The hosts assign this as homework: physically draw or digitally make the map to clarify dynamics and story opportunities.
